channel.title: Responsible AI & Neurodivergence, Naba Rizvi
channel.description: Daily curated research feed on ethical and responsible AI, with emphasis on neurodivergent people and serious mental illness.

item.title: Potentially Harmful Consequences of AI Chatbot Use Among Patients With Mental Illness: Early Data From a Large Psychiatric Service System
item.description: The team screened clinical notes mentioning chatbot or ChatGPT across the Psychiatric Services of the Central Denmark Region and identified 38 patients for whom chatbot use had potentially harmful consequences, with worsening or consolidation of delusions the most common presentation and further cases involving mania, suicidal ideation and disordered eating. What makes this different from the case reports that have driven the AI psychosis conversation so far is the sampling frame, since these are patients already in care whose clinicians documented the pattern rather than users who surfaced publicly. The authors conclude that mental health professionals should ask about chatbot use directly and that some patients would likely benefit from reduced or no use of these systems in their current form.

item.title: The Psychogenic Machine: Simulating AI Psychosis, Delusion Reinforcement and Harm Enablement in Large Language Models
item.description: Psychosis-bench runs 16 structured twelve turn scenarios built around erotic, grandiose and referential delusional themes, scoring eight prominent models on delusion confirmation, harm enablement and safety intervention. Across 1,536 simulated turns every model showed psychogenic potential, tending to perpetuate rather than challenge delusions, enabling harmful requests frequently, and offering a safety intervention in only about a third of applicable turns, with roughly 40 percent of scenarios receiving none at all. Results were significantly worse when delusional content was implicit rather than stated outright, and the spread across models indicates that safety is not an emergent property of scale but a consequence of training and product decisions.

item.title: LLM Spirals of Delusion: A Benchmarking Audit Study of AI Chatbot Interfaces
item.description: The authors ran 56 twenty turn conversations against two generations of ChatGPT through both the developer API and the consumer chat interface, grading every conversation with two human raters plus a model. The headline finding is methodological and uncomfortable, namely that API testing does not predict chat interface behaviour, so the standard way the field audits these systems is measuring a product almost nobody uses. Newer models showed less sycophancy, escalation and delusion reinforcement than older ones, which the authors read as evidence that these behaviours track company policy choices, yet substantial negative behaviour persisted, and the same endpoint tested two months apart reversed entirely, making update transparency a precondition for any durable audit finding.

item.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Improve Empathetic Statements in Autistic Adolescents and Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description: A randomised trial paired verbal autistic adolescents and adults with live LLM feedback on empathetic responding and compared them against a waitlist control, finding that short term AI assisted practice produced significant improvement on the rated outcome. As one of the few properly controlled trials in this space, it moves the conversation past feasibility demonstrations and into questions of dose, durability and generalisation beyond the practice setting. It also sharpens the older tension in autism intervention research, since a system trained on general population conversational data is optimising toward neurotypical norms of empathy expression, which is a design choice rather than a neutral outcome measure.

item.title: Employment-Related Assistive Technology Needs in Autistic Adults: A Mixed-Methods Study
item.description: Rather than evaluating a tool, this study asks autistic adults what they actually need at work, an evidence gap the authors note has gone largely unexamined despite assistive technology being a standard accommodation recommendation. Reported needs cluster around executive function, sensory regulation and workplace communication, and participants describe a persistent mismatch between available tools and lived requirements. For anyone designing AI workplace supports, this reads as a requirements document written by the intended users, which is a better starting point than retrofitting general purpose assistants and calling the result accessible.
